Daily Devotional

July 29

4 For every house is builded by some man; but he that built all things is God. 5 And Moses verily was faithful in all his house, as a servant, for a testimony of those things which were to be spoken after; 6 But Christ as a son over his own house; whose house are we, if we hold fast the confidence and the rejoicing of the hope firm unto the end. (Hebrews 3:4-6 KJV)

These verses have been comparing and showing that Jesus was superior to Moses in all things. Even though every house is built by a man, God was the ultimate builder of everything. Even though Moses was a faithful servant of the Lord, he was only a servant, whereas Jesus was the Son of God and the Creator of all things including Moses (Ephesians 3:9). The Creator is always greater than His creation, so Jesus was definitely greater than Moses in all ways.

Christ is over His own house, and we are His house, or body, the very Temple of God (1 Corinthians 3:16). As long as we stay faithful to the end, we will always be the house of the Lord. What a tremendous thought, to be the dwelling place of Jesus (Galatians 4:6) and the whole Godhead. Wow, we should stop and ponder that for awhile, as to have God Almighty living inside us is just hard to comprehend. Thank you Lord for Your coming and living in your Saints.

Devotional by Pastor Joe W. Green, www.Infinite-Faith.com

Simply put, just stopping the debt rising any further given its current amount would mean more than 50% of the entire Federal government's spending would have to be cut, stopped dead. The implications of that cut are not things Americans are prepared to live with, and they're not things Americans are even prepared to deal with. Anyone remember the "Ryan Plan" of the last couple of elections? He was running on fiscal conservatism, and the only plan he could stomach taking to the American people was to balance the budget -- not pay the debt down, mind you -- in 24 years.

This is not an issue of wasteful projects or corruption as such. Those are symptoms of a more systemic problem. The issue comes down to the old quote misattributed to Alexander Tytler: democracy survives only until people realise they can vote themselves benefices from public money. At that point, the democracy is inevitably doomed -- because when the public money starts to run out, politicians always resort to inflating public debt away. People will not give up the benefits they've received; this much is reflected in Cialdini's studies on human psychology, that revolutions are most common right after a regime gives a certain benefit or freedom and then moves to take it away, and they're invariably commanded by the spoilt children who last had that freedom.

The form of that eventual inflation and destruction of value may take different forms: they're not so subtle as to just print dollars anymore, they choose more CDO-ish stuff like 'quantitative easing', buying back bonds, etc, etc ... but the end result is the same. Eventually, people stop trusting the shitty currency they're holding because they become aware it has no value.

Smaller nations are not quite as sophisticated at the fiat shell game as the West is, which is why they periodically keep falling over in front of us: before Venezuela, there was Zimbabwe. There's always been Argentina, of course, which regularly forces its bond investors to keep taking haircuts on their bonds because they refuse to live within their means.

The only thing stopping a US debt default and hyperinflation is that there aren't any real alternatives for a world reserve currency at the moment. As Winston Churchill said, democracy is the worst possible way of governing people except for all the others (and the English have tried a few over the centuries, from monarchy to oligarchy to revolutionist autocracy). You might not trust the US dollar for value, but it's still an epically better bet than trusting the renmibi or the fucking rupee. Only when another currency reaches sufficient volume and sufficient reliability to challenge the US dollar is there realistically going to be a US dollar collapse. Maybe that will be bitcoin once they figure out how to make it a non-joke; but not for a while. As with the subprime crisis, everyone still has a vested interest in the merry-go-round continuing to roll. Unlike the subprime crisis, the body of people with a vested interest in the status quo is a global body. Only when there's an alternative or an outright irrational panic will things change.

As for those who say the debt is at manageable levels compared to GDP or other such measures, or indeed sneer at naysayers who have "wrongly" predicted the collapse of the US dollar: they're thinking of the debt-to-GDP level in the wrong way. The debt-to-GDP ratio is not a doomsday clock, hit 12 midnight and it's all over. The ratio is the snow 'red line' on a mountainside. When snow depth on a mountainside reaches a certain limit, we know from long experience that avalanches are much more frequent and much more likely to happen. Just because an avalanche doesn't happen the moment the snow exceeds the red line does not mean the warning is invalid: it means instead that skiing on that mountain is a pretty fucking stupid thing to do and you should refrain from such activities until the snow depth has dropped to historically safe levels again.
